study.title: 1 Corinthians 2 The Wisdom of God revealed in the Spirit
study.overview: In this chapter, Paul contrasts two ways of proclaiming the truth: trust in eloquence and human wisdom, and dependence on the power of God. He recalls that his preaching among the Corinthians was centered on Christ crucified, with apparent simplicity and weakness, so that the faith of the church might rely on divine power and not on human resources. Then it shows that there is a wisdom of God before hidden, now revealed by the Holy Spirit, inaccessible to natural reasoning without this revelation. The chapter culminates in the assertion that believers, because they have received the Spirit of God, can discern spiritual things and possess "the mind of Christ."

outline.title: Simple Preaching, Christ Crucified and Power of God
outline.explanation: Paul recalls that he did not reach the Corinthians relying on oratory orater orsuasion strategies. His focus was Jesus Christ and his cross. The fragility of the messenger did not overturn the message, because the aim was for the faith of the church to rest in the power of God, not in human capacity.

outline.title: Hidden wisdom, prepared by God and revealed by the Spirit
outline.explanation: Paul distinguishes the wisdom of the gospel from the wisdom of this world and its rulers. He calls this truth of mystery: something previously hidden, but now revealed to believers by the Holy Spirit. This revelation shows that the cross, rejected by the mighty, was part of God's plan since before the ages.

outline.title: The Spirit of God and the Mind of Christ
outline.explanation: Paul explains that only the Spirit knows the depths of God and it is through him that Christians understand the gifts of God. The natural human being does not welcome spiritual things, but whoever is spiritual can discern them. The conclusion is that believers have the mind of Christ, that is, they have been able to think according to the truth revealed by him.

study.context: Paul writes as an apostle to recall his first arrival to Corinth and his way of preaching there. The chapter responds to the fascination of the church by human prestige, eloquence and wisdom of this century. The background is the tension between the culture of appreciation by speakers and philosophers and the message of the cross, which seems weakness, but is the means chosen by God to save. The notes provided also relate Paul's remembrance in Corinth to the beginning of his ministry in the city and the contrast between human wisdom and the revelation of the gospel.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that Christian salvation and maturity depend on God's initiative, not of human intellectual superiority. The cross of Christ is the center of faith and the sufficient content of apostolic preaching. True wisdom is revealed by God in the gospel and can only be received by the Holy Spirit. Thus, the Christian faith is not based on techniques of conviction, but on the power of God, in the divine revelation and in the union of the believer with Christ. The expression "mind of Christ" does not suggest human omniscience, but a new inner disposition shaped by the Spirit, capable of discerning the truth of God.

scholarViews.insight: Paul did not trust in intellectual persuasion or a remarkable personality; his preaching was effective because the Holy Spirit acted, and faith should not rely on human wisdom, but on the power of God.
Christ, in his person and work, is the summary and substance of the gospel; therefore Paul decided to preach only Jesus Christ and this crucified one.
The wisdom proclaimed by Paul is a mystery previously hidden, but revealed by the Spirit of God; the rulers of this world did not know it, and therefore rejected the Lord of glory.

questions: In which areas do I still support myself more in appearance, skill, or arguments than in the power of God?
Does the center of my faith and my talk about the gospel continue to be Jesus Christ and his cross?
Have I sought to discern spiritual things by the light of the Holy Spirit or only by human criteria?
study.practice: This week, read the chapter carefully and ask God to reveal whether your trust is more in methods, influence or knowledge than on the power of the cross. By sharing your faith, speak of Christ with clarity and simplicity, without relying on verbal ornaments. Also take time to pray before making important decisions, asking for spiritual insight to think according to the mind of Christ and not according to the dominant logic of the world.
study.uncertainty: Matthew Henry's text provided is truncated from verse 6, but still allows you to safely identify the summarized idea used here. Notes do not provide extensive historical details; therefore, the context was described only on the basis of the chapter itself and the information explicitly mentioned in the comments.
